description:
Paired programming and explanation

Purpose

Practice explaining your reasoning out loud and reading someone else's code, not just producing your own. Pair programming is the Wednesday active work in this course's weekly rhythm (docs/course-ethos.md).

Do

  1. Work with a partner on the current week's problems (the same problems as assignments/A1-weekly-coding-practice.md, done together instead of solo). Take turns driving (typing) and navigating (reading, catching mistakes, asking questions); switch roles at least once per session.
  2. If you share one repository, each partner commits their own work. Your pair's git log must show a lines-of-code split no more lopsided than 80/20 — if one partner is consistently driving, that's a problem to fix before it's a grading problem.
  3. Record, in your own words: the problem, your approach, what changed in the code, how you tested it, and specifically what you contributed versus your partner.
  4. Note any outside help or AI/resource use — whose idea it was, and how you verified it.
  5. Present your progress to your partner or the class when scheduled.

What you submit: the paired-programming report

This is your own individual report, even if the code is shared — it's graded on your documented contribution, not the pair's combined output (docs/grading-model.md, 5% of the course grade). Include:

  • The problem and your approach, briefly.
  • What you personally wrote, fixed, or figured out (be specific — "helped with the loop" is not specific; "wrote the sentinel condition after our first version looped forever" is).
  • A pointer to the commit(s) or lines that back that claim up.
  • Anything you learned from watching or being corrected by your partner.

Separately: the Friday feedback report

If your section does Friday show-and-tell peer feedback, that's graded separately as its own 5% category — see assignments/A4-show-and-tell-reflection.md and docs/grading-model.md. Don't fold it into this report.

Support and integrity

If schedule or enrollment makes pairing impractical some weeks, this format may be dropped for that week — check with your instructor rather than skipping silently. Ask questions in class or office hours if you're unsure how to document a contribution split fairly.

description:
Friday feedback report

Purpose

Practice giving useful, specific feedback — the other half of the Friday Show and Tell slot in this course's weekly rhythm (docs/course-ethos.md). assignments/A4-show-and-tell-reflection.md grades what you demonstrated and how you reflected on your own work; this report grades the quality of the feedback you gave someone else, as its own 5% category (docs/grading-model.md). Authored 2026-08-06 (course_foundry prompt 026) -- previously referenced by docs/course-ethos.md, docs/grading-model.md, templates/T5-start-here.md, and both A3 and A4's "Separately:" sections, but never itself written.

Do

  1. During Friday Show and Tell, watch or read at least one classmate's demonstration (in-class discussion, presentation, or written/discussion post, depending on how your section runs it).
  2. Give them feedback in the moment (discussion) or in writing (post/ comment), specific to what they actually showed.
  3. Record, in your own words, what feedback you gave and why you gave it.

What you submit: the feedback report

This is graded on the quality of the feedback you gave, not on your own project (docs/grading-model.md, 5% of the course grade). Include:

  • Who/what you gave feedback on, briefly (no need to name classmates if your section prefers anonymity -- "the Investigation Bureau project I watched" is enough).
  • The feedback itself, in your own words -- not "looks good," a specific observation ("the loop recalculates the same total three times; a running variable would avoid that" is feedback; "nice job" is not).
  • Why you gave that feedback -- what you noticed, and why it seemed worth saying.
  • One thing you'd want the same kind of feedback on on your own project, next time.

Separately: the Show and Tell reflection

Your own project's demonstration and reflection are graded separately, under assignments/A4-show-and-tell-reflection.md. Don't fold that journal into this report -- this report is only about the feedback you gave someone else.

Support and integrity

If your section's Friday format doesn't include peer feedback some weeks (e.g. low attendance, a scheduling change), this report may be dropped for that week -- check with your instructor rather than inventing feedback you didn't actually give.
name: A7 — Friday Feedback Report (Week 02)

rubric.long_description: - **4 — Full credit:** Feedback names a concrete detail of the classmate's actual work (a specific choice, bug, or design decision) rather than a generic reaction. A reader who never saw the demo could tell roughly what was shown from the feedback alone. - **2 — Partial credit:** Feedback is topically relevant but stays vague ("the logic was a bit confusing") without naming the specific thing that was confusing. - **0 — No credit:** Feedback is generic praise/criticism with no identifiable connection to what was actually demonstrated ("looks good," "needs work").

- **3 — Full credit:** Explains *why* the observation mattered — what problem it would cause, or what it did well and why that's worth repeating. - **1.5 — Partial credit:** States the observation but not the reasoning behind it. - **0 — No credit:** No reasoning given, or the reasoning doesn't connect to the stated observation.

- **3 — Full credit:** Names one specific thing the student would want the same kind of feedback on, tied to their own project (not a generic "I should get feedback more"). - **1.5 — Partial credit:** Names something but it's generic or not clearly tied to their own project. - **0 — No credit:** Left blank, or unrelated to the feedback given.

description:
Show and Tell reflection

Purpose

Demonstrate one working program (or a meaningful honest attempt) and reflect on it — the Friday active-work slot in this course's weekly rhythm (docs/course-ethos.md).

Do

  1. Demonstrate one working program or meaningful attempt from this week — in discussion, a short presentation, or a written/discussion post, depending on how your section runs Show and Tell.
  2. Fill out the four-question journal below in your own words.
  3. If your section pairs this with peer feedback, see the Friday feedback report note below — it's graded separately.

The journal (10 points, current format)

Each question is graded individually, pass/fail:

# Question Points
1 What did you learn? 3
2 What else did you learn? 3
3 What could have gone better? 2
4 What made something feel special? 2

Answer each in your own words, specific to this week — "it went fine" does not pass; naming an actual moment, bug, or realization does. Any honest, specific answer passes; you don't need a success story for questions 3–4.

Separately: the Friday feedback report

If your section's Friday session includes peer feedback, the quality of feedback you gave is graded as its own 5% category (docs/grading-model.md), not as part of this journal. Keep the two separate: this journal is about your own work; the feedback report is about how well you responded to someone else's.

Support and integrity

This is low-stakes by design — the point is honest reflection, not a polished essay. If you're not sure what counts as "something to demonstrate" in a slow week, ask; a real attempt that didn't fully work is still valid material for questions 1–3.

description:
Weekly coding practice

Purpose

Reinforce this week's technical concept with real, working code, and show your process, not just your result. This is the "weekly topic reinforcement" artifact named in docs/course-ethos.md, worth 25% of the course grade (docs/grading-model.md).

This is fulfilled by the Reasoning Odyssey, not a required separate problem set

Every technical week of the semester is a Reasoning Odyssey week. There is no required textbook or external course (2026-08-12 reconciliation — CS1 has no required ZyBooks, no required Deitel, and no required CS50P enrollment). The week's concept and vocabulary come from Jeremy's own lecture/materials, with recommended no-cost supplements (CS50P lecture/notes where they genuinely fit, Python docs as reference) linked where useful — see docs/curriculum/course-sequence.md and the week-level resource map. You don't practice the concept by solving a required standalone problem set. You practice it by using that concept, that week, inside your own persistent Odyssey world.

  • Weeks with a gate (2–5, 7–8, 10–13): this assignment is that week's Odyssey Gate plus its open continuation. Do assignments/odyssey_gates/week-NN.md — nothing else is due under this name that week.
  • Checkpoint weeks (6, 9, 14): this assignment is that week's Reasoning Odyssey synthesis checkpoint. See assignments/A2-coding-odyssey-project.md.
  • Week 1, Week 15, Week 16, Week 17: no chapter-concept gate that week (Week 1 is universal across all five courses; Week 15 is a buffer/async week; Week 16 is the Farkle/ML fun week, no gate or checkpoint, and no graded weekly categories at all per the dead-days finding in docs/grading-model.md; Week 17 is finals) — see each week's own planning/week-NN.md for what's actually due.

This supersedes the previous framing of this file, which described an independent chapter-problem-set assignment running in parallel with the Odyssey. If you're looking at a planning/week-NN.md that still describes "chapter N practice" as a separate deliverable from that week's gate, the gate is the current source of truth — flag the planning file for an update rather than doing both.

Do

  1. If you want a concrete starting point before improvising your own scenario, work the suggested practice problem listed in that week's gate file first — it's the same concept, phrased as a plain practice problem with one version per genre. This is optional scaffolding, not a second assignment: do it privately for practice, then let it become (or inform) your actual gate submission. Skip it entirely if you don't need it.
  2. Do the current week's Odyssey Gate or checkpoint (see above for which).
  3. Submit working code, representative output, and a short explanation/report of what it does and why — applying this week's concept to your world, not in the abstract.
  4. Demonstrate it in discussion or show-and-tell when scheduled.
  5. Log it in your World Bible (assignments/A2-coding-odyssey-project.md).

Optional bonus practice — standalone problems

Reasoning Odyssey is the required technical practice path; skipping standalone problems never reduces your base grade. If you choose to also do optional standalone programming problems — instructor-owned problems, selected CS50P problems that align with what's actually been taught that week (not an entire CS50P problem set assuming concepts you haven't covered), or other already-vetted open/free exercises — you receive additive bonus/extra credit and keep that earned credit, even if you already satisfied the normal Odyssey requirement for the week. Do not copy/rehost third-party exercise text; linking to the problem is fine.

Decided 2026-08-12 (prompt 067): each of the 10 weekly-reinforcement weeks, one optional bonus-practice submission earns up to 5 flat bonus points, added as a 0-points-possible extra-credit item inside the Weekly Reinforcement Assignment Canvas group — capped at 10 counted weeks (50 points) for the whole semester. Full rationale and Canvas mechanics: docs/grading-model.md's "Bonus mechanism" section.

Grading — two axes, graded and reported separately

The gate (do this first)

Add a loop that processes an unknown or variable number of events in your world — sentinel-controlled (keeps going until some condition) or range-driven from real world state (not a hardcoded for i in range(3) with no connection to anything). Something repeated — harvests, patrols, transactions, log entries, whatever fits your genre — happens more than once because the loop says so, not because you wrote it out three times by hand.

  • [ ] A for or while loop is present and actually repeats (not a single-iteration loop standing in for an if).

  • [ ] An accumulator or running total/state changes across iterations (the loop does more than print the same thing N times).

Suggested practice problem (optional scaffolding)

description:
Final reflection

Purpose

Look back honestly on the semester — this is the final, in place of a traditional exam (docs/course-ethos.md, decided 2026-07-15). Worth 10% of the course grade (docs/grading-model.md).

Do

  1. Pick five prompts from the bank below (or propose an instructor-approved equivalent) — at least one from each of the four categories.
  2. Answer each in your own words. Full credit for any honest, specific answer you give, as long as you answer — this is a generous bar by design; vague or generic answers ("it was a good semester") don't earn full credit, but there's no single "correct" answer to chase. Scored with a real rubric and points (rubrics/A5-final-reflection-rubric.md, 10 points), not Canvas's plain pass/fail mechanism — that split exists specifically so a small optional bonus (below) has somewhere to attach.
  3. Share one favorite meme, quote, or moment from the semester — optional, but a nice way to close it out. This is just a nice way to close things out, not a graded rubric row.
  4. If your section's Reasoning Odyssey Week 17 work includes the Final Debrief and Judgment Log review (assignments/odyssey_gates/week-17.md), that is this reflection's Odyssey-specific half — don't write two separate reflections. Use one of your five prompts below for the rest of the semester's non-Odyssey material (classmates, career steps, general growth) so the two don't overlap.

Prompt bank — pick 5, at least one per category

Growth in programming - Describe the area where you grew the most as a programmer this semester, and what specifically helped you improve. - What's something you can do now with code that you couldn't do in Week 1? - What was the hardest concept to click, and what finally made it click?

A project or obstacle - Describe the biggest obstacle you overcame this semester and what kept you working at it. - Explain your favorite assignment and why it stuck with you. - Walk through one bug that taught you something real about how the computer (or you) actually think.

Learning habits and community - How were you able to help a classmate this semester? - Describe your best tools or habits for getting support when you were stuck. - What would you tell a friend taking this class next semester, that you wish someone had told you?

Next steps - What steps did you take this semester toward your career, and why did they matter to you? - Describe your plan for learning about job opportunities or companies you're interested in. - Name one specific thing (a certification, a project, a habit) you want to build on next semester, and why.

Bonus — genuinely specific and reflective (+2 pts)

Beyond the 10 base points, up to 2 extra-credit points are available for answers that name a specific, identifiable detail from your own semester — a moment, a bug, a person, a decision — rather than staying general. This is optional: you can earn all 10 base points with generous, honest-but- general answers, and only reach for these 2 points if you choose to go further. See rubrics/A5-final-reflection-rubric.md for the full scoring detail.

Support and integrity

This is graded generously and open-book/open-note/open-everything — take the time you need, and it's fine to revise and resubmit if you change your mind later. If a prompt above doesn't fit your semester, swap it for one that does; the categories matter more than the exact wording.

description:
Professional pathway artifacts

Purpose

Build real career-planning evidence over the semester — an unofficial transcript, degree plan, resume, target-role research, and online presence — not a one-time generic worksheet. This is the career-connection strand of the course (docs/course-ethos.md).

Do — staged across three weeks, not one big submission

Week 1 — establish baseline artifacts, ungraded (largely covered by semester_kickoff_week's A01–A09 set; see that repo for the actual handouts/rubrics once this course pulls from it directly):

  • Unofficial transcript / degree audit.
  • Advisor or progress check.
  • A preliminary degree plan (it's fine if it's rough).
  • A current resume, even incomplete.
  • Current GitHub and LinkedIn profiles.
  • An initial dream-job or target-role interest.

Week 14 — update pass, graded on its own (5% of the course grade) (paired with that week's GitHub work; rubric: rubrics/A6-week-14-update_rubric.md):

  • Refresh your dream-job/target-role research.
  • Do a skill-gap comparison against that role.
  • Update your resume.
  • Update GitHub and LinkedIn.
  • Update your degree plan if anything's changed.
  • Changelog/diff entry: write up what changed since your Week 1 baseline and why — not just what you edited, but the reasoning behind each change (why the target role shifted, why you reworded a resume line, why you added a project). This is the artifact this update pass is really graded on: the reasoning trail, not just the refreshed content.

Week 15 — completion and submission, graded on its own (5% of the course grade) (independent, asynchronous week — revise and organize what you've already built rather than starting from scratch; rubric: rubrics/A6-week-15-submission_rubric.md):

  • Submit the full, completed set: transcript/degree audit, degree plan, resume, GitHub/LinkedIn, target-role research, skill-gap analysis.
  • Add a brief reflection on your next steps — again, the reasoning behind each named step matters more than the list itself.

Week 16 does not carry this assignment — it's due in Week 15.

Why this is graded the way it is

This is where students establish practices they can keep using as they continue to grow in their profession — so both graded checkpoints reward the reasoning behind an artifact (why this target role, why this skill gap, why this change) over the artifact's polish. A rough resume with a clear, specific rationale for each change should score higher than a polished one with no visible reasoning behind it.

Support and integrity

If you're unsure what "instructor-approved equivalent" looks like for any artifact (e.g., you already have a finished degree plan from advising), ask rather than redoing work you've already done elsewhere — bring what exists and update it.
